opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I used to be quite a J person. When I was younger, especially as a student, I liked having a clear plan: what I'd do this semester, which problems I'd finish, what the next step in my career should look like. That gave me a sense of security.

But doing research slowly changed me. Research is fundamentally uncertain. You can write a beautiful plan at the start of a project, and three weeks later an experiment shows you something unexpected, and the most interesting direction is no longer on your plan at all. If you hold too tightly to the plan, you miss those surprises, and in my experience the surprises are where the real discoveries come from.

So my shift toward P wasn't a sudden personality change. It was more like adapting to the nature of the work. I started to see plans as hypotheses rather than commitments. I still set a rough direction, because I don't want to drift aimlessly, but I leave a lot of room to follow curiosity. If something looks weird or fun, I let myself spend a few days on it, even if it doesn't seem "productive" at the time.

There's also a more personal side. As I've gotten older I've become more comfortable with not knowing. Earlier, uncertainty felt like anxiety. Now it feels more like openness, like possibility. I think that's partly confidence: I trust that if I keep exploring honestly, something meaningful will come out of it, even if I can't predict exactly what.

So I'd describe myself now as a P with a J skeleton. There's some structure underneath, but on the surface I'm much more flexible, and I think that suits both research and life better for me right now.

r001.rationale: The response links his shift to research being uncertain and producing unexpected results, but it does not clearly say he recognized that many things in research or life are outside his control.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it started when I realized how much of my earlier life ran on plans that other people had written for me. In school, and even in the first years of my PhD, I was very J. I liked having a roadmap. I'd set a goal, break it into steps, and feel uneasy if the week didn't match the plan. That worked well for getting into good programs and publishing papers on schedule.

But at some point I noticed that almost nothing I was genuinely proud of came out of a plan. KAN, for example, came from a side conversation and a stubborn curiosity about splines that had no business being on my to-do list. The AI-for-physics work came from wandering between fields that my advisor and I weren't "supposed" to be exploring. Every time I looked back, the good things came from leaving space open rather than filling it.

So I started treating planning as a tool rather than an identity. I still have a sense of direction. I know roughly which questions I care about, and I know what I'm bad at. But I try not to lock the path. I let myself follow a strange result for a week, or read a paper far from my field, or say yes to a collaboration that doesn't fit cleanly. I've learned to tolerate the discomfort of not knowing exactly where something is going.

Part of it is also about research itself. Science is fundamentally a P activity. You're searching in a space you don't understand yet. If you decide in advance what the answer looks like, you mostly find what you already believed. Being more P, for me, means being more honest about that uncertainty and being willing to be surprised.

And there's a personal side too. Being very J gave me a sense of control, but it also created a lot of anxiety. Loosening that has made me calmer. I trust the process more now. I've seen enough times that if I stay curious and keep working, interesting things emerge, even if I can't say ahead of time what they'll be.

r001.rationale: The response links the shift to loosening plans, following curiosity, and accepting uncertainty, but does not clearly say he recognized that many things in research or life are outside his control.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as becoming more comfortable with uncertainty. Before, I might have wanted to figure everything out before taking the next step. Now I’m more willing to start with a rough direction and adjust as I go.

That doesn’t mean I don’t make plans anymore. It’s more that I don’t need reality to follow the plan exactly. Sometimes you discover what you actually want through doing things, and if you’ve decided everything in advance, you can miss that. So for me, becoming more P is about leaving room to change my mind.

r001.rationale: The response describes becoming comfortable with uncertainty and adjusting plans, but does not attribute the shift to recognizing that many things in research or life are outside his control.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it less as becoming a different person and more as becoming comfortable with uncertainty. I still like having a direction, but I don’t feel I need to decide every step in advance. Sometimes you only discover what’s worth doing after you start, and if you’re too attached to the plan, you can miss that.

So being more P, for me, means leaving room to respond to what actually happens. It doesn’t mean I’ve stopped caring about outcomes. I’m just more willing to let the path change.

r001.rationale: The response describes becoming comfortable with uncertainty and adapting the path, but it does not attribute the shift to recognizing that many things in research or life are outside his control.
